SK3501 A disposable is created in a local and never disposed

var x = new SomethingDisposable(); where the local never leaves the method and is never disposed.

CategoryLifetime
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floorC# 8.0
Since1.2
ReSharperNotDisposedResource (resharper_not_disposed_resource_highlighting)

Why

A disposable that is never disposed holds its handle until a finalizer runs, if it has one, and for ever if it does not. The visible symptoms — a file that cannot be reopened, a connection pool that empties, a socket in CLOSE_WAIT — appear far from the method that leaked and under load rather than in a test. The repair is one keyword, because C# 8's using declaration disposes at the end of exactly the scope the local already has.

Example

Instead of:

int Read(string path) {
    var stream = new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open);
    return stream.ReadByte();
}

Write:

int Read(string path) {
    using var stream = new FileStream(path, FileMode.Open);
    return stream.ReadByte();
}

When it does not fire

⚠ Ownership is the whole difficulty, so the rule reports only locals that provably keep it. The declaration must be a single declarator whose initializer is literally a new of a type implementing IDisposable — never a factory method, because Stream.Null and TextWriter.Synchronized return objects the caller does not own and nothing in the call tells them apart from a fresh one, and the local must never be returned, assigned to anything, passed as an argument or a ref/out, placed in an initializer or a collection expression, captured by a lambda or a local function, or yielded — every one of which is a way the object might outlive the method. It must also be read at least once, so that a declaration whose object is registered by its own constructor is not mistaken for a local nobody uses. ⚠ Ownership also travels outward, through what the object hands back. A read whose result is itself disposable withdraws the finding: device = backend.OpenDevice(options) never passes the backend anywhere and the device it produced is kept in a field, so disposing the backend at the end of the scope closes the device with it. So does a read inside a return expression, because return Task.Delay(10, source.Token) is not return stream.ReadByte() and nothing in the syntax tells them apart. ⚠ A constructor argument that is itself disposable disqualifies the finding, because new StreamReader(stream) takes ownership of stream and a using on the reader would close a stream the caller still owns — this is the guard that decides whether the rule is safe to apply, and it is the reason fixIsSafe can be true for the rest. ⚠ Task, Task<T>, System.Threading.Timer and System.Timers.Timer are excluded by name: a task is disposable and is never disposed by anyone, and a timer that is disposed at the end of the method that started it never fires. Methods that are iterators are skipped, and so is anything below C# 8, where the using declaration does not exist and the fix would have to re-indent a block.
